prompt: Linear search is said to examine about half a list on average. Which assumption makes that claim appropriate?

options.explanation: An absent target forces a full scan.
Sorting alone does not make requested target positions equally likely.
That gives constant work, not an average near half the list.

options.text: The target is present and equally likely at each position
options.explanation: Correct. Averaging those equally likely stopping points gives about half a scan.

workedExample: Average work needs a distribution. Uniformly chosen present positions balance early and late stopping points. Absent targets or a preference for early positions change that average. Under the stated uniform model, searching about half the list still gives linear growth.

prompt: Which of these statements about best, average, worst and expected case are **true**? Select all that apply. Assume distinct keys and ordinary two-way quicksort partitioning for the quicksort claims.

options.text: Randomised quicksort's expected Θ(n log n) time holds for every input, including sorted ones
options.explanation: True for every fixed input of distinct keys with fresh uniform random pivots. An adversary that can predict or adapt to random choices is outside that model.

options.text: Average-case analysis depends on assuming a distribution over the inputs
options.explanation: True. 'Average' means averaged over some assumed input distribution, often uniformly random. If real inputs are not like that (for example, nearly sorted), the average-case figure can mislead.

options.text: Adding an early return always improves worst-case asymptotic complexity
options.explanation: False. Some inputs may still take the old expensive path. Whether worst-case complexity improves depends on the algorithm and condition.

options.text: Quicksort that always picks the first element as pivot runs in Θ(n^2) on already-sorted input
options.explanation: True. Each partition separates only its pivot, leaving a range shorter by one. Adding those linear scans gives roughly half the square of the item count.

options.text: A fast best case is a strong guarantee about an algorithm's performance
options.explanation: False. Best case is easy to game: any algorithm can check for one special input first. It says nothing about inputs you will actually see.

workedExample: Separate the source of randomness from input choice. Uniform random pivots give the stated expected bound for every fixed distinct-key input. Average-case claims need an input distribution. A predictable end pivot on sorted input repeatedly leaves a nearly unchanged side. Early exits help the worst case only if they remove every input that attains the old expensive path.
